title: Leaving Slack
summary: Move a team's channels, history and integrations to a chat server you control, with one rehearsal and one clean cut-over.
audience: A team of 5 to 150 people on a Slack Free, Pro or Business+ workspace.
timeframe: Two to four weeks: a few days to set up and rehearse, one switch-over day, and a fortnight of keeping Slack readable.

stack.why: The most familiar layout for people coming from Slack, with an official import path. Install Team Edition explicitly, and read its licence note first.

stack.role: Team chat, if you want less noise
stack.why: Also has an official Slack importer, and no paid tier for server features. The steps below work for either; only the import tool differs.
Replaces huddles. Both chat servers can start a Jitsi call from a channel.

phases.title: Take stock
phases.intro: Find out what Slack is really doing for you beyond messages.

steps.title: Check what your plan lets you export
steps.detail: Free and Pro workspaces export public channels only. Business+ owners can also export private channels and direct messages. Decide now whether public history is enough, and tell the team what will and will not come across.

steps.title: List every app, bot and webhook
steps.detail: Go through the workspace's app management page. For each integration, write down what posts where and who owns it. Sort them into: has an equivalent, can use a generic webhook, or will be dropped.

steps.title: Archive dead channels
steps.detail: Archive channels nobody has used for months. Fewer channels means a faster import and a tidier start.

steps.title: List guests and Slack Connect channels
steps.detail: Shared channels with customers or partners cannot move. Agree with each external party what replaces them: email, a guest account on your new server, or keeping a small Slack workspace just for that.

steps.title: Choose Mattermost or Zulip
steps.detail: Try both for a few days with two or three colleagues, on a test server or a hosted trial. Mattermost needs almost no retraining. Zulip asks people to learn topics and repays it with far calmer channels. Check the features you need against each one's free edition.

steps.title: Install the server
steps.detail: Follow the official installation path on a fresh machine, with HTTPS and a proper host name. For Mattermost, make sure you install Team Edition: the default Entry edition limits visible history.

steps.title: Configure email and mobile notifications
steps.detail: Set up outgoing email for invitations and password resets, and enable the mobile push notification service. Test both on a real phone: missing notifications are the fastest way to lose people's trust in a new chat tool.

steps.title: Set up backups and test a restore
steps.detail: Back up the database and the uploaded files to a second location on a schedule, and restore them once onto a scratch machine.

steps.title: Decide how people will log in
steps.detail: Email and password works everywhere. If you want single sign-on, check that your chosen server includes it in the edition you are running before you promise it.

phases.title: Rehearse the import
phases.intro: Do the whole import once on a throwaway server. Problems found here cost nothing.

steps.title: Export the workspace
steps.detail: Run the export from Slack's settings and download the archive. It contains messages and links to files, not the files themselves.

steps.title: Fetch the uploaded files
steps.detail: Use slack-advanced-exporter to download attachments into the archive, along with user email addresses, which the importers need to match accounts.

steps.title: Import into a test server
steps.detail: For Mattermost, convert the archive with mmetl and run a bulk import. For Zulip, run its Slack import command. Expect the first attempt to reveal something: a user without an email address, an oversized file, a channel name that clashes.

links.label: Zulip: migrating from other chat tools

steps.title: Check the result with a colleague
steps.detail: Look at a busy channel, an old thread, a message with attachments and a message with emoji reactions. Note how long the import took: that is the length of your switch-over window.

phases.title: Switch over
phases.intro: Pick a quiet time. Friday afternoon works well.

steps.title: Announce the date
steps.detail: Give a week's notice in Slack itself and by email: the date, the new address, how to log in, and what will not come across. Ask people to save anything important from their direct messages.

steps.title: Freeze Slack and take the final export
steps.detail: Post a closing message in every active channel, restrict posting to admins where your plan allows, then export and fetch files exactly as rehearsed.

steps.title: Run the real import
steps.detail: Import into the production server, then invite everyone. Imported accounts are matched by email address, so people set a password and find their history waiting.

steps.title: Reconnect integrations
steps.detail: Work down the list from the first phase. Both servers accept Slack-format incoming webhooks, so for many tools you only need to paste a new URL.

steps.title: Get the apps onto every device
steps.detail: Share links to the desktop and mobile apps with the server address ready to paste. Check in with the least technical person on the team first.

steps.title: Keep Slack readable for two weeks
steps.detail: Leave the workspace open but silent. Note every time someone goes back for something: a pinned message, a private conversation, a file. Move what matters.

steps.title: Store the export archive safely
steps.detail: Keep the final export, with files, in your backups. It is your only record of anything that was not imported.

steps.title: Downgrade, then delete
steps.detail: Drop to the free plan at the end of the billing period. Delete the workspace once nobody has opened it for a month, unless you are keeping it for shared channels with outside parties.
